en: The Sūtra on the Fasting Rite, translated by the lay devotee Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi in the Wu Kingdom.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the palace of the Prime Minister in the eastern part of Śrāvastī. The Prime Minister...
Her mother’s name was Vīrā. Rising early, she bathed and donned her colorful robes; accompanied by her sons’ wives, she went forth, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
The Buddha asked Vīrā, “Why have you bathed so early?”
She replied,
"I wish to receive the precepts for the fast together with these women.
The Buddha said:
“There are three grades of fasting; which kind of fast do you prefer?
Vaira, kneeling with his right knee on the ground, said:
“I wish to hear what these three kinds of fasting are called.”
The Buddha said:
"First is the cowherd's fast, second is the Nirgrantha's fast, and third is the Buddhist fast. As for the cowherd's fast:

it is like a cowherd who seeks out fine water and grass to feed his cattle; at evening, returning home, he thinks of which pasture was most abundant and wishes that day would break so he may go there again."

If men or women of good family who have already received the precepts of fasting set their minds upon household affairs, profit, and industry, or think of fine food and drink to nourish the body, this is like the intention of that cowherd; they shall not obtain great merit, nor is it a great illumination.

"As for the Nigaṇṭha fast, on the fifteenth day of the month when it is time for the fast, one prostrates on the ground to receive the precepts of fasting and pays homage to the various deities within ten *yojanas*, saying:
'Today I am observing the fast; I dare not commit evil.
I no longer call myself a householder; there is no kinship between "self" and "other. Wives, children, slaves, and servants do not belong to me, nor am I their master.'"
However, as for their practice, they value the ornate and disparage the essential, lacking a correct mind; thus, when they reach the next life, their reputation remains as it was before.
Those who perform such ritual observances do not obtain great merit, nor do they attain great illumination.
"Regarding the Buddhist Dharma fast (*buddhadharma-upavāsa*), the disciples of the Way receive the eight precepts on the six days of the monthly fast.
What are the eight?

The first precept is to observe it for the duration of one day and one night, maintaining a mind like that of a true person (*satpuruṣa*). One must have no intent to kill and maintain compassionate thoughts toward all sentient beings. One must not harm even the smallest crawling creatures; one must not employ blades or staves, but instead contemplate how to bring benefit and peace, refraining from killing once more. One should practice this pure precept with a single-minded focus."

"The second precept is to observe it for the full duration of one day and night, with a mind like that of a true person (*satpuruṣa*). Free from the intent to covet or grasp, one should contemplate giving; one should give with joy, give with one's own hand, give with purity, give with reverence, and give without expectation. One should cast aside the mind of stinginess and greed, practicing this pure precept with single-minded devotion."

"The third precept is to observe it for one day and one night, with a mind like that of a true person (*satpuruṣa*): free from lustful intent and not thinking of the chamber; cultivating the holy life (*brahmacarya*), refraining from deviant desires, and not coveting forms with the mind; practicing this pure precept with single-minded devotion."

"The fourth precept is to observe it for one day and one night, maintaining a mind like that of a true person, free from any intent to speak falsely. One should contemplate with utmost sincerity, speak calmly and deliberately, refrain from hypocrisy and deception, ensure that heart and mouth correspond, and practice this pure precept with single-minded devotion."

"The fifth precept is to observe it for one day and one night, with a mind like that of a true person: not drinking alcohol, not becoming intoxicated, not becoming confused or disordered, and not losing one's resolve; removing thoughts of negligence and practicing with a single-mindedness according to the pure precepts."

"The sixth precept is to observe it for one day and one night, maintaining a mind like that of a true person (*satpuruṣa*), seeking no comfort, not adorning oneself with flowers or incense, not applying cosmetics or rouge, and refraining from song, dance, or entertainment; thus one should practice with a single-minded devotion according to the pure precepts."

"The seventh precept is to observe it for one day and one night, maintaining a mind like that of a true person (zhēnrén), seeking no comfort, not lying on a fine bed, but using a low bed or a grass mat, abandoning sleep and reclining to contemplate the Way of the sutras, practicing with single-mindedness as if observing the pure precepts."

"The eighth precept is to observe it for one day and one night, maintaining a mind like that of a true person (*bhūta-pudgala*). One should honor the Dharma by eating only at the proper time, eating sparingly to moderate the body, and refraining from food after midday. Thus, one practices with single-mindedness according to the pure precepts."
The Buddha told Vya:
"On the day one observes the fast, one should practice the five reflections.
What are the five?"
"First, one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
The Buddha is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, the Sugata, the Father of the World, the Anuttarapuruṣa, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, and is titled Buddha."

Those who practice this mindfulness of the Buddha completely eliminate ignorance, evil intentions, and the habit of anger; a virtuous mind arises spontaneously, and they come to delight in the Buddha’s deeds.
It is like using sesame oil and cleansing powder to wash one's head: the filth and turbidity are removed.
Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha while observing the fast are as pure as this; when others see them, there is none who does not respond with faith and admiration.
Second, one should be mindful of the Dharma.

One should fully comprehend and contemplate without distortion or forgetfulness the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment taught by the Buddha, knowing that these teachings serve as the illumination for the world.

One who contemplates the Dharma in this way completely eliminates ignorance, evil intentions, and the habit of anger; a virtuous mind arises spontaneously as they employ themselves in the practice of delighting in the Dharma.
It is like bathing the body with sesame oil and cleansing powder: the filth and impurities are removed.

Regarding those who practice mindfulness of the Dharma, their purity is such that no one who sees them fails to feel faith and admiration. Third, one should practice mindfulness of the Sangha. One should respectfully associate with and rely upon the community of the Buddha’s disciples to receive their wise teachings.

Within this assembly, there are those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and realized the realization of stream-entry; those who have attained the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and realized the realization of once-returning; those who have attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) and realized the realization of non-returning; and those who have attained the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*) and realized the realization of arhatship. These constitute the four pairs and eight classes of noble persons. All are perfected in virtue, perfected in concentration, perfected in wisdom, perfected in liberation, and perfected in the knowledge and vision of liberation. They are endowed with holy qualities and complete in their practice, and should be honored with joined palms as the field of merit for those above and below in heaven and earth.
In this mindfulness of the assembly, ignorance, malevolence, and the habit of anger are all eliminated, and a joyful mind naturally arises, performing the work of delighting in the assembly.
It is like washing clothes with pure ash: the stains and impurities are removed.
The virtue of one who maintains mindfulness of the assembly is such that all who see them will not fail to feel faith and joy.
"Fourth is mindfulness of the precepts.

One receives the Buddha’s precepts and upholds them with single-minded devotion; they are neither deficient nor violated, neither shaken nor forgotten. One establishes them well and guards them with care, is commended by the wise, has no cause for regret later, harbors no expectations, and is able to teach others impartially."

One who contemplates this precept eliminates all ignorance, evil intentions, and the habit of anger; a joyful mind arises naturally, and one delights in the practice of governing oneself through the precepts.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is removed, its brilliance shines forth.
Regarding those who maintain mindfulness of the precepts during the fast, their purity is such that all who see them will not fail to respond with faith and admiration.
Fifth, one should maintain mindfulness of the heavens.

One should reflect upon the first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; the second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the Yāma Heaven; the Tuṣita Heaven; the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. One should thus reflect upon them oneself:
"I possess faith, morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom; when my life ends and my spirit ascends to heaven, may I not lose this faith, morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom."
Those who contemplate this thought completely eliminate ignorance, malevolence, and the habit of anger; a joyful mind arises spontaneously, and they take delight in the work of governing the heavens.
It is like a precious gem that is constantly polished until it is clear and bright.
The purity of one who observes the fast while mindful of the heavens is like this:

by upholding the eight precepts and practicing the five reflections, one performs the fast for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, shares in the virtues of the heavens, extinguishes evil and promotes good, is reborn in the heavens hereafter, and ultimately attains Nirvana.
Therefore, the wise exert themselves and apply their minds to cultivate merit.

Thus it is, Vaira, that the blessings, protection, and illustrious reputation resulting from the fast are vast and far-reaching; even if these sixteen great kingdoms of the world were filled with incalculable treasures, they would not equal the merit of observing the Buddhist fast for a single day.
If one were to compare their merit, the sixteen kingdoms would be like a single bean.

The vastness and distance of the heavens are beyond description: fifty years in the human world now constitute one day and night in the first heaven; the lifespan in that first Cāturmahārājakāyika heaven is five hundred years, which corresponds to nine million years in the human world.
Those who observe the Buddhist fast will be reborn in this heaven.

One hundred years in the human realm constitutes one day and one night for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the lifespan in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is one thousand years, which corresponds to thirty-six million years in the human realm.

Two hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Salt Heaven (Lavaṇa-deva). The lifespan in the Salt Heaven is two thousand years, which corresponds to one hundred fifty-two million human years.

Four hundred years among humans constitute one day and one night in the Tuṣita Heaven; the lifespan in the Tuṣita Heaven is four thousand years, which corresponds to six hundred and eighty million years among humans.

Eight hundred years among humans constitute one day and night in the Heaven of No-Pride (Abhāsvara). The lifespan in the Heaven of No-Pride is eight thousand years, which corresponds to twenty-three billion four hundred million years among humans.

One thousand six hundred years among humans constitutes one day and one night for the Nirmāṇarati (Gods Who Delight in Creation) Heaven; the lifespan of the Nirmāṇarati devas is sixteen thousand years, which corresponds to nine billion two hundred and sixteen million years among humans.

If a person possesses faith, precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom, and observes the Buddhist fast according to the Dharma, then at the end of their life, that person’s spirit will be reborn in these six heavens of the gods, where they shall dwell in peace, security, and happiness.
"The wholesome is vast and manifold; I have spoken but a little of it. When ordinary people practice goodness, their spirits ascend to heaven and receive immeasurable blessings.
Having heard the Buddha's words, Vaira rejoiced and said, "Excellent, excellent!"
“World-Honored One!
The merit of the fast is most excellent and immeasurable; I pray that you will accept me as one who observes the Buddha’s precepts.
From this day forward, during the six fast days of each month, I shall exert all my strength to cultivate merit until death.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, they all received his teaching with joy.
The Sutra on the Fasting Observance Spoken by the Buddha.
